questions.q: If ${}^{n}C_4, {}^{n}C_5$ and ${}^{n}C_6$ are in arithmetic progression (A.P.), then the value of n is...
questions.solution:
Given that ^{n}C_4, ^{n}C_5, ^{n}C_6$ are in A.P.

2 \times ^{n}C_5 = ^{n}C_4 + ^{n}C_6$

$2 \times \dfrac{n!}{5!(n-5)!} = \dfrac{n!}{4!(n-4)!} + \dfrac{n!}{6!(n-6)!}$

Multiplying the entire equation by $\dfrac{6!(n-4)!}{n!}$:

$2 \times 6 \times (n-4) = 6 \times 5 + (n-4)(n-5)$

$12n - 48 = 30 + n^2 - 9n + 20$

$n^2 - 21n + 98 = 0$

$(n-7)(n-14) = 0$

$n = 7$ or $n = 14$

Answer: $7$ or $14$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $f(x) = x^{\dfrac{1}{3}}$

Let $x = 0.008$ and $\Delta x = -0.001$

$f(x) = (0.008)^{\dfrac{1}{3}} = 0.2 = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{3} x^{-\dfrac{2}{3}}$

$f'(0.008) = \dfrac{1}{3(0.008)^{\dfrac{2}{3}}} = \dfrac{1}{3(0.04)} = \dfrac{1}{0.12} = \dfrac{100}{12} = \dfrac{25}{3}$

Using the approximation $f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x) \Delta x$

$f(0.007) \approx \dfrac{1}{5} + \left(\dfrac{25}{3}\right)(-0.001)$

$f(0.007) \approx \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{25}{3000}$

$f(0.007) \approx \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{120}$

$f(0.007) \approx \dfrac{24 - 1}{120} = \dfrac{23}{120}$

Answer: $\dfrac{23}{120}$

questions.solution:
The expression ${}^{47}C_4 + \sum_{j=1}^5 {}^{(52-j)}C_3$ expands to ${}^{47}C_4 + {}^{51}C_3 + {}^{50}C_3 + {}^{49}C_3 + {}^{48}C_3 + {}^{47}C_3$.

Applying Pascal's identity ${}^{n}C_r + \binom{n}{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_r$ repeatedly:

Combining ${}^{47}C_4 + {}^{47}C_3$ yields ${}^{48}C_4$.
Adding ${}^{48}C_3$ gives ${}^{48}C_4 + {}^{48}C_3 = {}^{49}C_4$.
Continuing this pattern through ${}^{51}C_3$ produces ${}^{52}C_4$.

The expression simplifies to ${}^{52}C_4$, corresponding to option A.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given the sum $S = \binom{n}{0} + \frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{1} + \frac{1}{3}\binom{n}{2} + \ldots + \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n}{n}$, the general term is $\frac{1}{r+1}\binom{n}{r}$.

Using the identity $\frac{1}{r+1}\binom{n}{r} = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{r+1}$, the sum becomes $S = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n+1}{r+1}$.

Substituting $k = r+1$ yields $S = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} \binom{n+1}{k}$.

From the binomial theorem, $\sum_{k=0}^{n+1} \binom{n+1}{k} = 2^{n+1}$, so $\sum_{k=1}^{n+1} \binom{n+1}{k} = 2^{n+1} - 1$.

Thus, $S = \frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1}$.

Setting this equal to $\frac{1023}{10}$ gives $\frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1} = \frac{1023}{10}$.

Testing $n=9$ yields $\frac{2^{10} - 1}{10} = \frac{1023}{10}$, matching the given value.

The correct value is $n=9$, corresponding to option C.

questions.q: If ${ }^{15} \mathrm{C}_4+{ }^{15} \mathrm{C}_5+{ }^{16} \mathrm{C}_6+{ }^{17} \mathrm{C}_7+{ }^{18} \mathrm{C}_8={ }^{19} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{r}}$, then the value of r is equal to
questions.solution:
Given equation: $\binom{15}{4}+\binom{15}{5}+\binom{16}{6}+\binom{17}{7}+\binom{18}{8}=\binom{19}{r}$

Apply Pascal’s Identity $\binom{n}{r}+\binom{n}{r+1}=\binom{n+1}{r+1}$ consecutively:

$\binom{15}{4}+\binom{15}{5}=\binom{16}{5}$

The series becomes $\binom{16}{5}+\binom{16}{6}+\binom{17}{7}+\binom{18}{8}$

$\binom{16}{5}+\binom{16}{6}=\binom{17}{6}$
$\binom{17}{6}+\binom{17}{7}=\binom{18}{7}$

The expression simplifies to $\binom{18}{7}+\binom{18}{8}=\binom{19}{8}$

Thus $\binom{19}{8}=\binom{19}{r}$

This equality holds when $r=8$ or $r=19-8=11$

The solution corresponds to option D.
